rewrite.description: Lund's third album is where his ranch-country songwriting sharpened into the wry, detail-heavy style that defines his catalog, with songs about cattle trucks, small-town Alberta life, and rodeo culture. The Hurtin' Albertans back him with a loose, fiddle-and-steel sound closer to Western swing than Nashville polish, suiting listeners who like their country funny and specific.

Fiddle and pedal steel stay central, and Lund's drawl carries both the jokes and the rougher stories. It sits comfortably between traditional country and the alt-country audience.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to the American Bakersfield and honky-tonk tradition, filtered through Lund's Alberta ranch life.

rewrite.description: A more historically minded record than Lund's earlier albums, with songs touching on cavalry history and war alongside his usual rural character studies. It keeps the same fiddle-and-steel band sound while broadening his lyrical range beyond strictly agricultural subjects, and 'I Wanna Be in the Cavalry' shows how well his humor and history-buff streak mix.

It suits listeners who want character-driven Western country with some bite.

Sounds indebted to the Texas singer-songwriter lineage of Guy Clark and Townes Van Zandt, carried into the 2000s Americana boom.

rewrite.description: A more ambitious, occasionally psychedelic record than its predecessors, with the title track's Afghanistan-war narrative showing Carll stretching beyond barroom humor into something closer to protest storytelling. It still carries plenty of his trademark wit, but the arrangements are fuller and more varied than his earlier, sparer records.

A deliberate turn away from the comic persona of Carll's earlier records toward something quieter and more emotionally direct. The arrangements are spare and unhurried, letting his plainer, more vulnerable songwriting carry the record. It is for listeners who prefer his sincere side to his barroom jokes.

problems: lineage is peer resemblance, marked Documented

rewrite.lineage: Sits alongside Justin Townes Earle and Caitlin Rose as a Nashville outsider working in classic country forms, a kinship of approach rather than a direct link.

rewrite.description: Welder is a rootsier, more rock-inflected record than Balls, drawing on Cook's rural family background. Songs like 'El Camino' and 'Mama's Funeral' balance humor with genuine hardship, keeping her classic-country vocal style intact even as the arrangements broaden.

A darker, more experimental record made after a stretch of personal upheaval, trading some of Cook's earlier humor for grittier, occasionally psychedelic textures. It still carries her distinctive voice but pushes further from straight honky-tonk than any of her previous work, with heavier guitars and a slower groove.

rewrite.description: Jewell's debut is a spare, twangy record steeped in old country, blues, and folk, named for a rural corner of her home state of Idaho. Her cool, understated vocal delivery contrasts with the record's occasional noir atmosphere, closer to Neko Case's early work than to mainstream Nashville. It set out her blend of retro country and roots-blues.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to the same pre-rock country and rockabilly revivalism as Wanda Jackson, filtered through a hushed, understated vocal delivery distinct from most alt-country peers.

rewrite.description: One of Jewell's most fully realized records, mixing surf-tinged guitar tones with pedal steel and her usual restrained vocal style. The title nods to her taste for minor-key melodies over straightforward major-key country, and the songs lean moody and cinematic.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to classic country and rockabilly, given a cool, cinematic treatment in the manner of other retro-minded 2000s Americana singers.
Continues Shires's evolution from sideman fiddler to singer-songwriter, sounding of a piece with the literate Americana she would later pursue with the Highwomen.

rewrite.description: Written while Shires was pregnant with her first child, this record deals with new motherhood and domestic life with unusual directness, still anchored by her fiddle playing and clear, unadorned voice. It is one of her most personal records, trading some of the earlier albums' darker atmosphere for warmth.

problems: unsupported recording location and burnout biography

rewrite.description: Another Country is a quieter, more reflective record than Merritt's first two albums, trading horns and rock energy for spare, intimate arrangements. It sounds like a songwriter stepping back to reassess her direction, and it marked her move from Lost Highway to Fantasy Records.

problems: lineage wrongly ties to Lost Highway roster; resemblance only

rewrite.description: Edwards's debut pairs plainspoken, often bruising lyrics about failed relationships and small-town frustration with a scrappy, guitar-driven alt-country sound. 'Six O'Clock News' turns a local news story into a stark character study, setting the tone for her direct, unsentimental songwriting. It is for anyone who likes Lucinda Williams-style grit with a Canadian accent.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to Lucinda Williams's gritty, guitar-driven alt-country, carried into the Canadian scene.
Sounds indebted to Whiskeytown and Lucinda Williams, with Edwards's Canadian alt-country pushing toward bigger rock hooks.

rewrite.description: A broader, more ambitious record that takes on subjects beyond personal relationships, including war and violence against women, while keeping Edwards's plainspoken lyrical style intact. It mixes rock energy with country songcraft, and 'Alicia Ross' shows how far her character writing had come.
rewrite.lineage: Extends Edwards's alt-country songwriting into more political territory, sounding of a piece with the guitar-driven work of Neko Case and Lucinda Williams.

rewrite.description: Co-produced with Justin Vernon of Bon Iver, Voyageur moves considerably further from straight alt-country into hushed indie-folk textures, with synths and strings softening the edges. It is her most polished and least twangy record, though the plainspoken, heartbroken songwriting remains.

Whitmore's debut is a stark, solo banjo-and-guitar record steeped in gospel, blues, and old-time Southern folk, sung in a weathered baritone far older than his years. It draws on the same well of hardship as Charlie Poole and old hymnals. It found an unlikely early audience through the punk and hardcore scene that first booked him.

A continuation of Whitmore's stripped-down banjo-and-guitar sound, dealing heavily with mortality and loss. The record's stark arrangements leave nowhere to hide his weathered baritone, giving it an unusually raw, funereal quality that will suit listeners who came to old-time music through punk.

Whitmore's first record for Anti- fills out his usual banjo-and-gospel base with fuller arrangements, alongside more explicitly political lyrics addressing class and power. It keeps his weathered baritone and old-time phrasing intact even as the sound grows louder. It marked his move from the punk-adjacent Southern Records to the more Americana-facing Anti- roster.

rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to the Woody Guthrie-to-Dylan folk songwriting lineage, closer to folk revivalism than to twangy alt-country proper.

rewrite.description: Rose's latest record continues her steady evolution from spare old-time country toward a fuller, more contemporary alt-country sound, with pedal steel carrying much of the color. It keeps the plainspoken directness of her earlier work, and the songwriting stays centered on wanting and self-knowledge rather than any single narrative arc.

problems: overstated career claim (earlier country albums exist)

rewrite.description: After beginning in the punk band Attack in Black, Romano turned to a meticulous, almost archival recreation of 1960s countrypolitan honky-tonk, down to period-accurate arrangements and vocal phrasing. Songs about heartbreak and drinking are delivered with an unusually precise ear for classic country's conventions, making it a treat for Nashville Sound devotees.

problems: label move and labelmate claims unsupported

rewrite.description: Romano's precise recreation of classic Nashville countrypolitan production continues here, with lush strings, pedal steel, and fiddle behind his crooning, deliberately old-fashioned vocal. Songs of heartbreak and drinking are sequenced like a lost 1960s LP. It is for listeners who want countrypolitan played straight rather than as pastiche.

Continuing the psychedelic country-rock direction of Mosey, this record leans further into dense, string-laden arrangements and a more surreal lyrical style than Romano's earlier, plainer honky-tonk records. It keeps his precise ear for vintage production while applying it to stranger, more baroque songwriting.
rewrite.lineage: Continues Romano's move from honky-tonk purism toward psychedelic country-rock that sounds indebted to Gram Parsons-era Cosmic American Music.

problems: doubtful Austin placement at the time

rewrite.description: Rose's breakthrough record is a lean, hook-driven honky-tonk set with a vintage, early-1960s Nashville sound, built around her clear, unfussy voice. Songs balance genuine heartbreak with a wry sense of humor closer to classic country than modern Americana introspection.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds of a piece with the classic honky-tonk revivalism of Daniel Romano and other Canadian traditionalists working a vintage Nashville sound.

rewrite.description: Rule 62 sharpens Rose's classic-country sound with fuller, more polished arrangements while keeping the vintage honky-tonk foundation intact. Pedal steel and fiddle frame her clear voice, and the songs move breezily between heartbreak and wry humor.
rewrite.lineage: Extends Rose's vintage honky-tonk revivalism, sounding akin to the classic-country reverence of Daniel Romano's records.

rewrite.description: Waldon's Oh Boy Records debut, signed by John Prine, sharpens her honky-tonk sound with a full touring band and songs addressing addiction, home, and the opioid crisis in her native Kentucky. It keeps her plainspoken, twang-heavy style intact, with pedal steel and fiddle front and center.

rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to the 1970s Nashville songwriter tradition, of a piece with contemporaries like Caitlin Rose working outside the mainstream industry.
Sounds indebted to the deadpan, funny-sad songwriting of John Prine and Tom T. Hall, sharing a Nashville outsider scene with Andrew Combs and Caitlin Rose.

rewrite.description: Now recording under his given name, Fritz sharpens his deadpan songwriting on a record with a fuller, more polished country sound than his earlier Corndawg records, pedal steel and fiddle filling out the arrangements. Songs continue to find humor in mundane, specific details of everyday life without tipping into novelty.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to John Prine's deadpan, funny-sad songwriting, now with cleaner production.

rewrite.description: A more polished, expansive record that keeps Chisel's gospel-soul foundation while adding fuller string and piano arrangements. His hushed, church-steeped vocals stay at the center, and the songs lean toward slow-burning testimony rather than barroom twang. It suits listeners who like their Americana closer to soul and gospel.

rewrite.lineage: Sits at the punk-and-psychobilly edge of Bloodshot's insurgent-country roster, sounding closer to X-style cowpunk than to conventional twang.

rewrite.description: Favourite Colours pushes the Sadies' reverb-heavy, spaghetti-western guitar sound toward denser, more layered arrangements, with pedal steel and harmonies around the twin guitars. The interplay between brothers Dallas and Travis Good remains the core, swinging from surf-tinged instrumentals to cosmic-country songs. It is a strong pick for anyone who likes their alt-country guitar-first.
rewrite.lineage: Extends the Sadies' instrumentally driven, cosmic-country sound; the band's work backing Neko Case and Jon Langford ties them to the wider Bloodshot-adjacent scene.

rewrite.description: A more introspective, song-focused record than the band's earlier instrumental-showcase albums, with the Good brothers' voices given more room. It keeps the Sadies' signature reverb-heavy guitar interplay while giving the songwriting more emotional weight than usual, and the tempos lean relaxed and breezy.

Released months after Dallas Good's sudden death in 2022, Colder Streams became the band's final album with its full classic lineup, adding an unintended elegiac weight to its already reflective songwriting. It keeps the band's reverb-heavy, twin-guitar cosmic-country sound intact through to the end, making it a fitting if unplanned closing statement.

rewrite.lineage: Grows out of the hard country of Merle Haggard and George Jones, filtered through Simpson's bluegrass background; it set the stage for the genre-hopping he started on Metamodern Sounds.

Follows Metamodern Sounds' genre-blurring instinct further from Nashville orthodoxy, sounding indebted to Muscle Shoals soul and Waylon Jennings-era concept records.

A deep-cut companion for fans who want the full breadth of his songbook reimagined.

rewrite.description: A sprawling triple album presenting the same set of songs three ways: the stark 'Hallelujah' versions, the full-band 'Jubilee' versions, and the psychedelic, synth-warped 'Joyful Noise' versions. It's a divisive, maximalist gospel-and-recovery concept record that tests how far Childers can stretch his own songs, from 'Way of the Triune God' to a take on 'Angel Band'. Best heard as a whole to appreciate the arranging experiment.
rewrite.lineage: Builds on Long Violent History's gospel streak while pushing toward psychedelia that recalls the cosmic-country turns of Sturgill Simpson, a mentor figure throughout Childers' career.

rewrite.description: A leaner, more traditional-sounding record after the sprawl of Hounds to Heaven, built around plainspoken love songs and a Kris Kristofferson cover. Sounds indebted to Bob Wills-style Western swing, connecting the neo-outlaw revival back to Texas swing traditions.

rewrite.description: Crockett's self-released debut is raw, busker-rough country-blues, recorded cheaply and reflecting years spent playing on street corners. It's the least polished record in his catalog but already shows his talent for sounding like a lost 1960s recording. A curio for completists tracing his rise.

rewrite.lineage: Refines the vintage honky-tonk sound of his early records, closer to 1950s Nashville than to contemporary country, with phrasing that sounds indebted to George Jones.

rewrite.description: This album mixes honky-tonk with warm horn arrangements and soul touches, reflecting Crockett's Gulf Coast, blues-adjacent version of country music. It's a smoother, more Southern-soul-inflected record than his earlier releases. Good for listeners who like their country with a little Stax in the mix.

A loose outlaw-revenge concept record, The Man from Waco is Crockett at his most Marty Robbins-indebted, with strings and pedal steel framing a narrative about murder and pursuit across the Texas landscape. It is possibly the strongest distillation of his cowboy-noir persona.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to Marty Robbins' gunfighter ballads and Texas outlaw mythology, continuing the classic-country storytelling strand within the neo-outlaw scene.

rewrite.description: $10 Cowboy sticks to Crockett's classic honky-tonk-and-cowboy-song formula, with pedal steel and fiddle behind road-worn songs about touring life and hard-won success after years of busking. A confident, mid-career victory-lap record for fans of his vintage sound.

The latest entry in Crockett's remarkably steady run of vintage-toned country albums, keeping the classic-country formula that has defined his 2020s output, with pedal steel, a laconic drawl, and road songs. A dependable addition for listeners already following his catalog.

Produced by the Black Keys' Dan Auerbach, this record sharpens Lane's outlaw-cool persona with fuller, twangier production and a run of kiss-off songs. Telecaster and pedal steel drive it, and her drawl stays sly and unbothered. Rowdy, glamorous, unapologetic.
rewrite.lineage: Builds on Walk of Shame's honky-tonk sass with more polished outlaw-revival production, of a piece with the wave that includes Margo Price and Colter Wall.
Pulls the honky-tonk outlaw persona toward imagery that recalls Gram Parsons's Cosmic American Music and desert-rock atmosphere.

rewrite.description: Produced by Josh Homme, this record roughs the sound back up with fuzzier guitars and a harder rock edge under the honky-tonk bones, and the lyrics carry a tough, kiss-off attitude. It's her rowdiest, least polished record in years. Good for listeners who want the scene's grittier, rock-adjacent side.

rewrite.description: Jinks' breakout record pairs straight outlaw-country songwriting with a heavy, low-slung band sound and that cavernous baritone, giving it more weight than most neo-traditional records. rewrite.lineage: Jinks came to country after playing in a metal band; the record sounds indebted to Waylon Jennings-style outlaw country, an unusually heavy entry in the revival.

rewrite.description: His first release through a larger label, Lifers keeps the same heavy-baritone outlaw sound while polishing the production, aimed squarely at the blue-collar audience that built his career through word of mouth. A representative later-period Jinks record, anthemic and whiskey-soaked.

rewrite.description: Produced by Rodney Crowell, Emerson's self-titled second album sharpens his storytelling, including songs that confront his Choctaw-Apache heritage head-on. The arrangements stay understated, fingerpicked guitar and fiddle keeping the lyrics in front. A high point of the lane's Texas-songwriter wing.
rewrite.lineage: Rodney Crowell's production ties Emerson directly to the outlaw-era Texas songwriter generation; the writing itself sounds indebted to Guy Clark and Townes Van Zandt.

rewrite.description: Produced by Shooter Jennings, this record fills out Emerson's sound with more full-band arrangements, pedal steel, and a touch of cosmic-country shimmer while keeping his sharp, plainspoken lyric focus. A good bridge between his stark early work and a bigger studio sound.

rewrite.description: Waldon keeps the same classic-country foundation here while widening into reflections on grief, land, and belonging. The arrangements stay traditional and unhurried, with pedal steel and fiddle around her thick drawl. A mature, settled record from one of the scene's steadiest traditionalists.

rewrite.lineage: Extends the Prine-indebted storytelling of Between the Country with fuller band arrangements, continuing the Kentucky-storyteller strand of the scene.

problems: unsupported scene tie to Vincent Neil Emerson

rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to classic honky-tonk storytelling (George Jones, Roger Miller), with an unusual, almost yodeling vocal style.

rewrite.description: Walker's second album keeps the same compassionate character studies while widening into songs about his own life on the road. The pedal-steel-and-twang arrangements stay close to classic honky-tonk, and his cracked, yelping voice does the heavy lifting. A slightly more personal companion to his debut.

The third in Walker's loose trilogy of character-study honky-tonk albums, with songs sketching a cast of small-town characters over pedal steel and twang. His cracked, yelping voice remains the draw. A fitting closer to his early run of story-driven honky-tonk songwriting.

Shoulders keeps his yodeling old-time foundation here while broadening the band arrangements slightly, still centered on rural class politics and environmental concern delivered with dry humor. Harmonica and a deep, rolling baritone anchor it. A good survey point for his whole catalog.

rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to old-time folk and cowboy-poetry traditions, connecting the Guthrie-to-Townes folk songwriting line to the current DIY neo-traditional scene.

rewrite.description: Carlisle's breakout record blends old-time folk, cowboy songs, and queer rural storytelling into a warm, generous set of songs about found family and small-town life. 'Vanlife' and 'When the Pills Wear Off' show his range from wry humor to raw testimony, all over fingerpicked guitar and harmonica.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to the folk-songwriting line running from Guthrie through Gillian Welch, with sharper storytelling.

rewrite.description: A fuller-band follow-up to Peculiar, Missouri, Critterland widens Carlisle's old-time-and-cowboy-song palette with fiddle and bigger arrangements while keeping his focus on rural queerness, addiction, and community. It is his most ambitious record, and a strong entry point for the folk-songwriting side of the lane.

Carlisle's latest record leans further into reflective, spiritual songwriting while keeping the old-time and cowboy-song instincts of his earlier albums. Fiddle and fingerpicked guitar keep it hushed and warm, continuing his run of community-minded folk-country records.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to the folk-songwriting line running from Guthrie through Gillian Welch.

rewrite.description: Southern Star pushes Cobb's warm, low-key groove further toward swampy, gospel-tinged soul, with pedal steel and harmonica drifting through unhurried arrangements. Independently released on his own label, it suits listeners who like their country slow, humid, and a little psychedelic.
rewrite.lineage: Deepens the Southern country-soul lineage of his earlier albums with gospel shading that sounds indebted to Bobby Charles-style swamp soul.

rewrite.description: Godwin's debut is West Virginia storytelling country, full-band and radio-friendly but rooted in specific Appalachian place names and coal-country memory. Pedal steel and harmonica color the arrangements. A strong entry point for the Appalachian storytelling wing of the scene.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to the Southern storytelling rock line from Skynyrd through Drive-By Truckers, with a specifically West Virginia focus.

rewrite.description: Godwin's second album widens the sound with fuller rock arrangements while keeping the same coal-country and family storytelling focus. It's more emotionally direct and anthemic than his debut. A fitting sophomore step for fans of contemporary Appalachian rock-country.

rewrite.description: Hedley's second album trims the strings-heavy countrypolitan gloss of Mr. Jukebox for a brighter, Telecaster-and-fiddle sound closer to early-1990s neotraditional country. It keeps his classicist songwriting instincts, with heartbreak and drinking songs sung in a clean, easy drawl. A slightly looser companion to his debut.

Wyatt's breakthrough record draws directly on her own time in jail on a robbery charge, delivering plainspoken outlaw-country songs about crime and consequence with an easy, unaffected twang. Telecaster and pedal steel keep it lean. It's one of the most literal 'outlaw' records of the whole lane.
rewrite.lineage: Echoes the classic outlaw-country confessional tradition, including Merle Haggard's prison songs, from a contemporary perspective.
Moves Wyatt's outlaw-confessional songwriting toward soul and rock textures, an arc that resembles Margo Price's later albums.
Sounds indebted to the Southern California country tradition of Buck Owens and the Bakersfield sound, filtered through LA's contemporary Americana scene.

rewrite.description: Top's debut is a near-perfect recreation of late-1980s and early-1990s neotraditional country, produced by Carson Chamberlain and delivered with a tasteful, unshowy Telecaster-and-fiddle band and a warm, drawling tenor. Songs like 'Sounds Like the Radio' and 'I Never Lie' play the old archetypes straight, without irony.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to the late-1980s neotraditionalist country of Randy Travis and Keith Whitley, carrying that revival into the 2020s.

rewrite.description: A double-bassist steeped in old-time, blues, and Western swing, Carper mixes vintage upright-bass swing with plainspoken country songwriting delivered in a warm, unhurried voice. It sounds like a lost 1950s record more than a contemporary one. A quiet standout of the classicist wing of the scene.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to Western swing and pre-war country, connecting the neo-traditional revival to honky-tonk-era bass-driven dance music.

rewrite.description: Butts' second album is polished, radio-adjacent country with a stronger traditionalist streak than most Music Row product, built around plainspoken songs about relationships and self-worth. Pedal steel colors the arrangements, and her drawl carries a steely, anthemic edge. It sits closer to Texas-leaning Nashville country than to the rawer honky-tonk end of the lane.
rewrite.lineage: Sits between the neo-traditional revival and the more mainstream Red Dirt and Texas-country scene of acts like the Turnpike Troubadours.

rewrite.description: Roadrunner! is Butts' most ambitious record, a concept-driven set mixing full-band country-rock with theatrical, narrative songwriting. Its storytelling and steel-guitar textures keep it inside the neo-traditional lane despite crossover production, and the duets and darker Southern gothic turns make it a distinctive, genre-bending entry.
rewrite.lineage: Combines musical-theater storytelling with contemporary Texas and Red Dirt country production, a hybrid of the lane's narrative focus and arena-Americana sound.
Sounds of a piece with the plainspoken, rural-life storytelling of Colter Wall, from an explicitly Montana ranching perspective.

rewrite.description: Dean's second album is confident, big-voiced Texas honky-tonk about aging, ambition, and small-town escape, delivered with a strong alto closer to Lacy J. Dalton than to any indie-country trend. Telecaster and pedal steel keep it firmly in the dancehall. A sturdy, underrated entry in the current Texas honky-tonk revival.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to classic Texas honky-tonk, sitting alongside revivalists like Joshua Ray Walker.

rewrite.description: Kevin Patrick Sullivan's Field Medic record moves from four-track bedroom folk toward fuller arrangements, with pedal steel and drum machine behind his hushed voice. He keeps his diaristic, deadpan-honest songwriting about touring, drinking, and love, and the songs still feel like private notes.

A sequel to an early Field Medic release that trades folkier elements for 808s, synths, and trap-inflected production. Sullivan keeps his confessional, journal-like lyricism and deadpan delivery, so the drum machines frame the same diary entries rather than replacing them.

This Field Medic record blends Sullivan's folk roots with the electronic textures of light is gone 2, pairing drum machines with lo-fi guitar. The diary-like songs stay deadpan and often bleak, for listeners who like confessional songwriting with a bedroom-recording feel.

Oak Park poet-songwriter Kara Jackson's grief-steeped debut, written after the death of a close friend, sets impressionistic short tunes alongside long, slow stretches given room to breathe. Her low, deadpan voice and fingerpicked guitar carry lines that are often funny and devastating at once.

A Philly DIY veteran's self-titled record of unflinching confessional folk about addiction and recovery, recorded plainly with little studio polish. Hushed vocals and fingerpicked guitar keep everything close and bleak, for listeners who want songwriting with nothing between them and the singer.

rewrite.description: Anaïs Mitchell, Eric D. Johnson, and Josh Kaufman's debut as a trio reworks traditional British and American folk ballads into warm, harmony-driven arrangements. Fingerpicked guitar and close three-way singing give old songs like 'Deep in Love' and 'The Roving' a hushed, lived-in glow.

The trio's second album moves from strict traditional-ballad reworkings toward more original songwriting, keeping the same warm three-way harmony blend. Fingerpicked guitar and gentle, gospel-tinged arrangements frame songs like 'Gone by Fall' and 'Someone to Weep for Me'.

A double LP and Bonny Light Horseman's most expansive record, splitting introspective and more communal songs across two discs. The close harmonies and fingerpicked arrangements remain the core, with duets between Mitchell and Johnson carrying much of the weight.
rewrite.lineage: The trio's third full-length, continuing their blend of traditional folk revival and original songwriting among members of Fruit Bats and Muzz.
Grows out of the raw, homemade folk of Bad Debt and Haw into a fuller country-rock sound that sounds indebted to the Grateful Dead and the Band, which Taylor kept refining on later Merge albums.
